{{Short description|Group whose Cayley graph is an initially subamenable graph}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2026}}
[[File:Sofic.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Two balls of radius 2 in the [[Cayley graph]] of the [[dihedral group]] <math>D_4</math>. Both balls contain 7 of the 8 group elements and are [[graph isomorphism|isomorphic]] as [[edge coloring|edge-colored graph]]s. Furthermore, for ''any'' radius <math>r</math> and <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, we can use the approximating graph <math>G_0</math> as the full Cayley graph itself, where the set <math>W</math> of all vertices satisfies <math>|W|/|V| = 8/8 = 1 > 1-\varepsilon</math>. Since all 8 vertices have isomorphic <math>r</math>-balls (by the vertex-transitivity of Cayley graphs), <math>D_4</math> is sofic.]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''sofic group''' is a [[group (mathematics)|group]] whose [[Cayley graph]] is an initially [[amenable group|subamenable]] graph, or equivalently a [[subgroup]] of an [[ultraproduct]] of finite-rank [[symmetric group]]s such that every two distinct elements of the group have distance 1.{{sfnp|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|2010|p=276}} They were introduced by [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Gromov]] as a common generalization of [[amenable group|amenable]] and [[residually finite group|residually finite]] groups.{{sfnp|Gromov|1999}} The name "sofic", from [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]] {{lang|he|סופי}} 'finite', was later applied by [[Benjamin Weiss|Weiss]],{{sfnp|Weiss|2000}} following his use of the word as a generalization of finiteness in [[sofic subshift]]s. A '''non-sofic group''' is a group that is not a sofic group.

The class of sofic groups is [[closure (mathematics)|closed]] under the operations of taking subgroups, [[Group extension|extensions]] by amenable groups, and [[free product]]s. A [[finitely generated group]] is sofic if it is the [[Direct limit|limit]] of a sequence of sofic groups. The limit of a sequence of amenable groups (that is, an initially subamenable group) is necessarily sofic, but there exist sofic groups that are not initially subamenable groups.{{sfnp|Cornulier|2011}}

Gromov proved that Sofic groups are [[surjunctive]].{{sfnp|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|2010|p=276}} That is, they obey a form of the [[Garden of Eden (cellular automaton)|Garden of Eden theorem]] for [[cellular automaton|cellular automata]] defined over the group ([[dynamical system]]s whose states are mappings from the group to a [[finite set]] and whose state transitions are [[Curtis–Hedlund–Lyndon theorem|translation-invariant and continuous]]) stating that every injective automaton is surjective and therefore also [[reversible cellular automaton|reversible]].{{sfnp|Ceccherini-Silberstein|Coornaert|2010|p=56}}

==Existence of non-sofic groups==

In 2026, artificial intelligence research company [[OpenAI]] announced a machine-checkable [[proof by construction]] of the existence of a non-sofic countable discrete group.<ref>{{cite web |date=2026-08-01 |title=Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science |url=https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/ |access-date=2026-08-02 |website=[[OpenAI]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sparkes |first=Matthew |date=2026-08-03 |title=OpenAI announces solutions to 10 longstanding maths problems |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2582793-openai-announces-solutions-to-10-longstanding-maths-problems/ |url-status=live |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20260803211956/https://www.newscientist.com/article/2582793-openai-announces-solutions-to-10-longstanding-maths-problems/ |archive-date=2026-08-03 |access-date=2026-08-04 |work=[[New Scientist]] |language=}}</ref> The existence of such groups was previously an open question. Researchers in the field have raised the possibility that key ideas in the proof were taken from their unpublished research, about which they had non-public conversation with OpenAI's chat bots.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://finance.biggo.com/news/e25efed9-378a-4987-a29c-856268143b07|title=OpenAI's Math Breakthrough Hit by Fresh Plagiarism Storm: Dresden Mathematician Publishes Emails Alleging 20 Years of Work Was Stolen}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/11/on-the-existence-of-non-sofic-groups/|title=
On the existence of non-sofic groups}}</ref> [[Navier–Stokes priority controversy|Similar concerns]] were raised about OpenAI's announcement of a solution to the Navier-Stokes [[Millenium Prize Problem]].
